topic: The Binary Secret of the Tower of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students and early undergraduate computer science students

sections.title: The Puzzle Setup: Rules of the Game
lecture_lines: The Tower of Hanoi has three pegs and disks.
Rule one: move only one disk at a time.
Rule two: no larger disk atop a smaller one.
Goal: move the stack to a different peg.
Binary counting reveals the most efficient solution.
animations: Show three pegs labeled A, B, and C with 3 disks stacked on A.
Animate the top disk (Disk 1) moving from Peg A to Peg B.
Try to move Disk 2 on top of Disk 1; flash red #FF0000 to indicate an invalid move.
Move Disk 2 to Peg C, showing a valid move following the rules.
Highlight the entire stack on Peg A and the empty Peg C as the target.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Binary Counting as a Pulse
lecture_lines: Binary counting uses a sequence of flipping bits.
Each bit position represents a power of two.
Observe which bit flips during each increment.
animations: Display binary '000' and transition to '001' in white #FFFFFF, highlighting the flipped rightmost bit in yellow #FFFF00.
Transition from '001' to '011' through '010', highlighting bits that change in green #00FF00.
Display three lightbulbs toggling at different frequencies (1, 2, 4) to represent the binary pulse in white #FFFFFF.

sections.title: The Mapping: Disks as Bits
lecture_lines: Map each disk to a specific binary bit.
The smallest disk corresponds to the rightmost bit.
Second disk maps to the second binary bit.
The largest disk maps to the third bit.
Move the disk when its bit changes value.
animations: Align 'Disk 1', 'Disk 2', and 'Disk 3' with bits '2^0', '2^1', and '2^2' in magenta #FF00FF.
Highlight Disk 1 and the first bit '2^0' simultaneously in magenta #FF00FF.
Highlight Disk 2 and the second bit '2^1' simultaneously in magenta #FF00FF.
Highlight Disk 3 and the third bit '2^2' simultaneously in magenta #FF00FF.
Show bit '2^0' flipping and the corresponding Disk 1 moving from Peg A to Peg C.

sections.title: The Directional Logic: Where to Move?
lecture_lines: Move disks in a consistent cyclic pattern.
Odd total: move the smallest disk A-C-B-A.
Even total: move the smallest disk A-B-C-A.
animations: Draw Pegs A, B, and C in a triangle with clockwise arrows A to C to B.
Label the path 'Odd n = 3' and highlight the A to C arrow.
Move Disk 1 from Peg A to Peg C following the highlighted arrow.

sections.title: Synthesis: Solving the 3-Disk Puzzle
lecture_lines: Increment the binary counter to identify each move.
The rightmost bit flip determines which disk moves.
Step four flips the third bit for the largest disk.
Follow the sequence to reach the final state.
Seven moves complete the three-disk puzzle.
animations: Create a split-screen with 'Binary Counter' on left and 'Towers' on right.
Binary increments from '011' to '100'; highlight the changed 3rd bit in cyan #00FFFF.
Move Disk 3 from Peg A to Peg B on the right side of the screen.
Sequence through the remaining steps quickly until the counter reaches '111'.
All disks are now stacked on Peg C; the screen glows gold #FFD700.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of 2^n - 1
lecture_lines: Binary counting perfectly models the Tower of Hanoi.
Total moves equal two to the power n minus one.
Each move is encoded in the binary sequence.
animations: Display the formula 'M = 2^n - 1' in large cyan #00FFFF text.
Show n = 64 and the resulting massive number of moves below it.
Text '585 Billion Years' appears and slowly scales up in white #FFFFFF.
